blocks.text: When white light falls on a compound it may be absorbed completely, and the compound looks black; it may be reflected or transmitted completely, and the compound looks white; or part of it may be absorbed and the rest reflected, and the compound shows a colour. The colour we see is the complementary colour of the light absorbed: a complex that absorbs yellow light appears violet.

blocks.alt: A colour wheel of six equal sectors: Orange at the top, then Yellow, Green, Blue, Violet and Red going clockwise. Opposite sectors are complementary colours.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.6: Colour wheel showing complementary colours (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.6).

blocks.title: d-d transition
blocks.text: An electron in a lower-energy d orbital absorbs light and is promoted to a higher-energy d orbital. The light absorbed has energy equal to the gap: delta E = h nu = hc/lambda, where h is Planck's constant, nu the frequency, c the speed of light and lambda the wavelength. The unabsorbed light passes on and gives the colour.
Effect of different ligands on delta E and colour

The ligand affects the size of the splitting. Ligands such as NH3 and CN- cause large splitting; ligands such as Cl- and I- cause small splitting. A larger delta E means light of higher frequency (shorter wavelength), in the violet or blue region, is absorbed, so the complex looks yellow or orange; a complex that absorbs low-energy red or orange light looks blue or green. Ligands can be ordered by the splitting they cause, from high to low delta E:

blocks.title: Ligand order (large to small splitting)
blocks.text: CN- > en > NH3 > H2O > OH- > Cl- > Br- > I-
